title: Provide customer care in the perishable produce export industry

lessons.title: Customers and service standards in the export chain
lessons.html:
Who the customers are

In the export chain almost everyone is both a supplier and a customer. A packhouse serves growers (who supply fruit and pay packing fees) and exporters (who buy and market the packed fruit). An exporter serves overseas importers and retailers, and also its growers. Service providers such as cold stores, transporters and inspection services have exporters and packhouses as customers. Internal customers, such as the dispatch team relying on the cold store, matter too.

What export customers value

  • Consistent quality to specification, arrival after arrival.
  • Reliability of volumes and timing; programmes with retailers depend on it.
  • Transparency: early warning of problems such as a smaller crop, hail damage or a delayed vessel.
  • Accurate documentation that clears customs and phytosanitary checks without delay.
  • Responsiveness to queries and claims, across time zones.
  • Compliance with food safety, ethical and environmental standards.
  • Fair commercial dealing: clear terms, timely payment and honest account sales to growers.

Setting service standards

Service standards make good customer care measurable and consistent. Examples:

  • respond to every buyer email within one working day;
  • send shipping documents within an agreed time after the vessel sails;
  • notify the buyer of any quality concern before shipment;
  • issue grower packout reports within a set time after packing;
  • acknowledge claims within 24 hours and respond with evidence within a set period.

Measure performance against these standards and share results with the team.

Cultural awareness

Export customers come from many cultures. Communication styles, expectations about formality, negotiation and holidays differ. Learn the basics of each market's business culture, be aware of time zones and public holidays such as Chinese New Year or Ramadan that affect demand and office hours, and always remain courteous and professional.

lessons.title: Building relationships and managing claims
lessons.html:
Building long-term relationships

  • Communicate proactively: share crop estimates, quality updates and shipping schedules before customers ask.
  • Visit and host: buyer visits to farms and packhouses build trust; show your systems and people.
  • Listen to feedback: arrival reports and retailer scorecards tell you what to improve.
  • Keep promises: it is better to under-promise and deliver than to over-promise and disappoint.
  • Have one point of contact for each key customer, with a back-up.
  • Record interactions in a customer database so that knowledge is not lost when staff change.

Managing quality claims

Claims are part of the fresh produce trade. How they are handled often matters more to the relationship than the claim itself.

  1. Acknowledge the claim quickly and professionally.
  2. Request evidence: an independent survey report, photographs, temperature downloads, pallet numbers and arrival dates.
  3. Investigate internally: check PPECB inspection results, packhouse QC records, cooling and loading temperatures, container logger data and transit time.
  4. Identify the cause: pre-harvest, packing, cold chain or handling at destination.
  5. Respond with facts: agree a fair settlement where the cause lies with you, or explain clearly with evidence where it does not.
  6. Learn: record the claim and take corrective action to prevent repeats.

Example

A UK importer reports soft, decayed plums on arrival. The exporter acknowledges the same day, requests the survey report and downloads the container logger. The data shows the container ran several degrees above the set point for four days because of a unit fault. The exporter shares the evidence, supports the importer's claim against the shipping line, and keeps the importer's trust.

Handling difficult conversations

Stay calm, focus on facts, avoid blaming individuals, and look for solutions. Escalate commercial decisions to the right level. Follow up in writing to confirm what was agreed.

Key points

  • Customers include growers, exporters, importers, retailers and internal teams.
  • Export customers value consistency, reliability, transparency and accurate documents.
  • Set measurable service standards and track them.
  • Communicate proactively and respect cultural differences.
  • Handle claims quickly, with evidence, fairness and learning.
